title: Gothia
capsule: Gothia denotes the territory of the Goths north of the lower Danube and across the western Pontic steppe, attested from around the 3rd century CE. The Goths — divided into the Thervingi west of the Dniester and the Greuthungi to the east — raided Roman Dacia and Moesia repeatedly before Emperor Claudius II defeated them at Naissus in 269. Their territorial cohesion collapsed in 375–376 when the Hunnic advance from the east overran the Greuthungi and forced the Thervingi to seek asylum across the Danube into Roman territory, ending Gothic political unity on the steppe.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The geographic extent of Gothic settlement in the 3rd–4th centuries is reconstructed chiefly from the Chernyakhov archaeological culture and Roman literary sources (Jordanes, Ammianus Marcellinus); boundaries are broad estimates rather than administratively defined frontiers, making territorial precision conjectural.
